Succeeded
suk-sēd'-ed
v. (came after and took the place of; in the Authorized Version, dispossessed and inherited — never “prospered”)
Latin succedere, to go under or come after. The modern sense of prospering is absent from the Authorized Version; all three occurrences mean to take another people's place in their land, and the Hebrew is literally inherited.

Biblical Definition

All three occurrences stand in one passage of Deuteronomy, where Moses is explaining why Israel must not attack Edom, Moab or Ammon. “The Horims also dwelt in Seir beforetime; but the children of Esau succeeded them, when they had destroyed them from before them, and dwelt in their stead; as Israel did unto the land of his possession, which the LORD gave unto them” (Deu 2:12). And of the Ammonites and the giants before them: “A people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims; but the LORD destroyed them before them; and they succeeded them, and dwelt in their stead” (Deu 2:21). The point Moses is making is startling. God had given Seir to Esau and Ar to the children of Lot, and had cleared out the previous inhabitants for them, exactly as He was about to do for Israel in Canaan. Israel therefore may not touch a foot of it. The God of Israel is not a tribal deity who manages only His own people's conquests; He assigns lands to nations who do not know Him — the doctrine Paul preached at Athens, that God hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation. Israel's title to Canaan was a gift, and so was Edom's to Seir, and the same Giver protected both.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines succeed as to follow in order, to take the place which another has left; and notes the sense of obtaining the object desired as a distinct use.

expand to see more

SUCCEED, v.t. To follow in order; to take the place which another has left.

1. To follow; to come after; to be subsequent or consequent.

2. To prosper; to obtain the object desired; to accomplish what is attempted or intended.

SUCCESSION, n. A following of things in order; a series of persons or things following one another in time or place.

Key Scripture

Deu 2:12 — "The Horims also dwelt in Seir beforetime; but the children of Esau succeeded them, when they had destroyed them from before them, and dwelt in their stead; as Israel did unto the land of his possession, which the LORD gave unto them."

Deu 2:21 — "A people great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims; but the LORD destroyed them before them; and they succeeded them, and dwelt in their stead:"

Deu 2:22 — "As he did to the children of Esau, which dwelt in Seir, when he destroyed the Horims from before them; and they succeeded them, and dwelt in their stead even unto this day:"

Modern Corruption

Success is read into a word that means dispossession; and God's rule over the nations is shrunk to His rule over the church.

expand to see more

The English word has drifted so far that a reader meets succeeded in Deuteronomy 2 and hears achievement, where Moses means that one people took another people's land. That drift matters beyond the lexicon, because it is a small instance of how the vocabulary of success has colonized Christian speech generally — successful ministries, successful marriages, a successful life — importing a measure Scripture does not use. The Bible's categories are faithful and unfaithful, fruitful and barren, wise and foolish. Joseph in prison was not successful; he was blessed, which is a different word and a different scale.

The doctrine in the passage is worth as much as the lexicography. God assigned Seir to Esau and Ar to Lot's children, dispossessed nations to make room for them, and forbade Israel to take an inch of it. He governs the nations that do not worship Him as truly as the nation that does — the Most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will. Israel had no ground for supposing her title was superior in kind to Edom's; both were gifts, and the Giver defended both. That is a sharp word to any people inclined to read its own borders as a divine endorsement.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yarash (H3423), to take possession, to dispossess, to inherit; tachath (H8478), in the place of, instead of; gebul (H1366), border.

expand to see more

Hebrew yarash (H3423) — to seize, possess, dispossess, inherit; the verb rendered succeeded in Deuteronomy 2:12, 2:21-22, and everywhere else possess or drive out.

Hebrew tachath (H8478) — under, in place of, instead of; dwelt in their stead.

Hebrew Chori (H2752) — the Horims (Horites), the cave-dwellers of Seir before Edom.

Hebrew 'Anaqim (H6062) — the Anakims, the tall people whose report terrified the spies in Numbers 13.

Greek horothesia (G3734) — the fixing of boundaries; Acts 17:26, God determined the bounds of their habitation.

Usage

"“The children of Esau succeeded them… and dwelt in their stead”."

"“The LORD destroyed them before them; and they succeeded them” — for Ammon."

"“As he did to the children of Esau” — the reason Israel must not touch Seir."
